summary:
**12.1.2 Single-stage detectors.** Around 2015, researchers started using a *single* deep learning model to jointly predict bounding-box coordinates and their labels — a **single-stage detector**. The main families are **RetinaNet**, **Single Shot MultiBox Detectors (SSD)** and **You Only Look Once (YOLO)** — named after the meme, on purpose. Single-stage detectors, especially recent YOLO versions, are significantly faster and more efficient than two-stage ones, with only a *minor potential tradeoff in accuracy*. YOLO is arguably the most popular detector today, particularly for real-time use; a new version usually appears every year, each tending to come from a different organization.

**12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch.** The authors warn that building a detector is an undertaking — not because the theory is hard, but because of the amount of code needed to manipulate bounding boxes and predicted outputs. To keep it simple they recreate the **very first YOLO model (2015)**; there are 12 YOLO versions at the time of writing, but the original is simpler.

**12.2.1 Downloading the COCO dataset.** The training data is **COCO** (*Common Objects in Context*), one of the best-known detection datasets: real-world photos from many sources with human annotations — object labels, bounding boxes and full segmentation masks. The chapter ignores the masks and uses only boxes. The 2017 version is about **18 GB**, the largest dataset in the book, so downloading it is "a good chance to take a breather".

**Listing 12.1** begins: it imports `keras` and `keras_hub` and calls `keras.utils.get_file("coco", "http://images.cocodataset.org/zips/train2017.zip", extract=True, ...` to download and unzip the training images. The call is closed, and the annotations archive downloaded, at the top of p.357.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Around 2015, people began using a single deep learning model to jointly predict box coordinates and labels — a single-stage detector. The main families are RetinaNet, SSD and YOLO; the YOLO name deliberately echoes the meme.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The defining change versus R-CNN is the removal of a separate proposal step: one network, one forward pass, outputs both where and what.

concepts.name: Single-stage detector
concepts.definition: A single deep learning model that jointly predicts bounding-box coordinates and their labels.
concepts.intuition: Look once at the whole image and output all boxes.
concepts.technical: No separate region-proposal stage; families include RetinaNet, SSD and YOLO.
concepts.significance: Much faster and more efficient than two-stage detectors with a minor potential accuracy cost; dominant for real-time use.
concepts.misconception: That single-stage detectors are much less accurate — the book calls the trade-off minor.

concepts.name: YOLO (You Only Look Once)
concepts.definition: A family of single-stage detectors, the first from 2015; 12 versions existed at the time of writing.
concepts.intuition: The name says it: one look (one forward pass) per image.
concepts.technical: The chapter's simplified version divides the image into a grid and predicts one box, confidence and class per cell (p.360).
concepts.significance: Arguably the most popular detector, especially for real-time applications.
concepts.example: New versions appear roughly yearly, often from different organizations.
concepts.misconception: That 'YOLO' refers to one fixed architecture — it is a family of quite different models.

concepts.name: COCO dataset
concepts.definition: Common Objects in Context: real-world photos with human-created labels, bounding boxes and segmentation masks.
concepts.intuition: A standard benchmark of everyday scenes with many objects per image.
concepts.technical: The 2017 training images come as `train2017.zip`; annotations come separately as JSON (p.357). This chapter uses only boxes and labels.
concepts.significance: At 18 GB, the largest dataset in the book.
concepts.example: Most images in chapter 12 come from COCO (footnote 1).
concepts.misconception: That COCO is only a detection dataset — it also includes full segmentation masks.

code.title: Downloading the 2017 COCO dataset (first part)
code.original_code:
import keras
import keras_hub

images_path = keras.utils.get_file(
    "coco",
    "http://images.cocodataset.org/zips/train2017.zip",
    extract=True,
code.what_it_does: Imports Keras and KerasHub and starts a `keras.utils.get_file` call that downloads the COCO 2017 training-image archive and extracts it, storing the local path in `images_path`. The listing continues on p.357, which closes the call and downloads the annotations archive into `annotations_path`.

line_explanations.explanation: Import Keras and KerasHub (KerasHub is not used by these lines; it is needed later in the chapter).
`keras.utils.get_file` downloads a file into the Keras cache directory (by default `~/.keras/datasets`) unless it is already there, and returns its local path.
`"coco"`: the name to store the download under in the cache.
URL of the 2017 training images zip on the official COCO server.
`extract=True` unzips the archive after download; the returned path then points to the extracted content. The call's closing parenthesis is on p.357.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: network access and disk space (about 18 GB for the dataset). Output: `images_path`, a string path whose `train2017/` subdirectory holds the JPEG images (used on p.357 as `images_path + "/train2017/" + image["file_name"]`).
code.algorithm: Check cache → download if missing → extract archive → return path.
code.theory_link: Supplies the raw photos for training the YOLO detector; labels and boxes come from the separate annotations file.

parameters.name: fname ("coco")
parameters.role: Local name for the cached download.

parameters.name: origin (URL)
parameters.role: Where to download the archive from.

parameters.name: extract
parameters.role: Whether to unpack the archive after downloading.

pitfalls: The download is large; an interrupted download may need the cached partial file removed before retrying.
Make sure the cache directory's disk has room for both the zip and the extracted images.
Exact return-path semantics of `get_file` with `extract=True` changed across Keras versions; if the `train2017/` path is not found, print `images_path` and inspect it.

deeper.title: Why 'not theoretically complex' still means a lot of code
Two-stage vs. single-stage at a glance
deeper.body:
| | Two-stage (R-CNN) | Single-stage (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet) |
|---|---|---|
| Proposal step | Yes (Selective Search / RPN) | No |
| Passes per image | Classify thousands of proposals | One network pass |
| Speed | Slow | Significantly faster |
| Accuracy | High | Minor potential trade-off |
| Real-time / embedded | Mostly unsuitable | The usual choice |

takeaways: Single-stage detectors (RetinaNet, SSD, YOLO) predict boxes and labels jointly with one model; they emerged around 2015.
They are significantly faster than two-stage detectors with a minor potential accuracy cost; YOLO is the most popular for real-time use.
The chapter rebuilds the original 2015 YOLO because it is simpler than the 12 later versions.
Detection code is mostly box bookkeeping rather than complex theory.
COCO 2017 (18 GB) provides labels, boxes and masks; only boxes and labels are used.
Listing 12.1 downloads and extracts the training images with `keras.utils.get_file`; the annotations follow on p.357.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT named on the page as a family of single-stage detectors?
questions.explanation: Faster R-CNN is a two-stage detector (p.355). RetinaNet, SSD and YOLO are the single-stage families listed here.

questions.question: What trade-off do single-stage detectors make relative to two-stage detectors, according to the page?
questions.answer: Significantly faster speed and greater efficiency, with a minor potential tradeoff in accuracy.
questions.explanation: Quoted from the second paragraph of 12.1.2.

questions.question: Why do the authors choose to recreate the original 2015 YOLO instead of a recent version?
questions.answer: Because the original is simpler to work with, and building a detector already requires a lot of box-manipulation code; keeping the model simple keeps the chapter manageable.
questions.explanation: Stated in the opening paragraph of 12.2.

questions.question: Which COCO annotations does the chapter use?
options: Bounding boxes (with object labels), not masks
questions.answer: Bounding boxes (with object labels), not masks
questions.explanation: The authors disregard the segmentation masks and use just bounding boxes; labels are also used (p.357). Captions aren't mentioned.

questions.question: In listing 12.1, what does `extract=True` do, and what does `images_path` hold?
questions.answer: It makes `get_file` unpack the downloaded zip; `images_path` holds the local path of the downloaded/extracted COCO images, later joined with `/train2017/` and a file name.
questions.explanation: See the code explanation; usage of `images_path` appears in listing 12.2 on p.357.

questions.question: How does COCO's inclusion of both masks and boxes relate to the argument on p.354?
questions.answer: It illustrates that segmentation annotations are a superset of detection annotations: the same dataset can train a segmenter, but the cheaper boxes are all a detector needs.
questions.explanation: An inference connecting the dataset description to the strict-superset argument.

questions.question: Can you explain to someone why YOLO is called a single-stage detector and why that makes it suitable for real-time video?
questions.answer: It predicts all boxes and labels in one pass of one network instead of classifying thousands of proposals, so it can keep up with incoming frames.
